# Vehicle Peripheral Moving Object Detection Device

## Overview

The present device is directed to a system for detecting moving objects in the vicinity of a vehicle through the acquisition and analysis of peripheral image data. The device comprises three primary functional components: an image acquisition unit, an image extraction unit, and a moving object information determination unit, each of which will be described in detail below.

## Image Acquisition Unit

The device includes an image acquisition unit configured to acquire a peripheral image surrounding the vehicle. This peripheral image captures the environment immediately adjacent to and surrounding the vehicle, thereby enabling the subsequent detection of moving objects—such as pedestrians, cyclists, or other dynamic entities—that may be present in the vehicle's vicinity. The image acquisition unit may utilize one or more cameras, sensors, or imaging devices positioned at various locations on the vehicle to ensure comprehensive coverage of the surrounding area, including front, rear, and side regions as necessary for effective monitoring.

## Image Extraction Unit

Once the peripheral image has been acquired, an image extraction unit processes this image data to identify and extract relevant portions depicting a moving object. Specifically, the image extraction unit is configured to extract at least one of the following: a first image showing the upper body of the moving object, or a second image showing the lower body of the moving object. This bifurcated extraction approach allows the device to focus on distinct anatomical or structural regions of a detected moving object, which may enhance detection accuracy and provide more granular data for subsequent analysis.

### First Image Classification

The first image, which depicts the upper body of the moving object, may be further categorized into one of two distinct subtypes based on the completeness of the captured region:

- **'1-1'-st image**: This subtype represents an instance in which the first image depicts the entire upper body of the moving object, providing a complete representation of this body region without occlusion or truncation.
- **'1-2'-nd image**: This subtype represents an instance in which the first image depicts only a partial view of the upper body, such as may occur when the moving object is partially obscured, positioned at the edge of the camera's field of view, or otherwise only partially visible within the acquired peripheral image.

### Second Image Classification

Similarly, the second image, which depicts the lower body of the moving object, may be extracted as one of two distinct subtypes:

- **'2-1'-st image**: This subtype represents an instance in which the second image depicts the entire lower body of the moving object, capturing this region in its complete form.
- **'2-2'-nd image**: This subtype represents an instance in which the second image depicts only a partial view of the lower body, which may result from similar occlusion or field-of-view limitations as described above with respect to the first image.

This dual-tier classification scheme—distinguishing between complete and partial representations for both the upper and lower body images—allows the device to accommodate a wide range of real-world imaging conditions, including variable lighting, occlusion by other objects, and the moving object's position relative to the image acquisition unit's field of view.

## Moving Object Information Determination Unit

Following the extraction and classification of the first and/or second images, a moving object information determination unit utilizes this extracted image data to determine information pertaining to the moving object. Specifically, this unit analyzes the first image and/or the second image to ascertain at least one of the following: (i) the presence of the moving object within the vicinity of the vehicle, and/or (ii) the position of the moving object relative to the vehicle.

By leveraging the classified image subtypes—whether representing complete or partial views of the upper and/or lower body—the moving object information determination unit is able to make informed determinations even in cases where only partial image data is available. This capability enhances the robustness and reliability of the overall detection system, enabling accurate identification and localization of moving objects under a variety of real-world conditions, including scenarios involving partial occlusion or limited visibility of the moving object within the acquired peripheral image.

## Summary

Through the coordinated operation of the image acquisition unit, image extraction unit, and moving object information determination unit, the disclosed device provides a comprehensive framework for detecting and characterizing moving objects in the vicinity of a vehicle. The hierarchical classification of extracted images into upper and lower body representations, each further subdivided into complete and partial subtypes, enables flexible and robust processing of peripheral image data, ultimately supporting accurate determination of the presence and position of nearby moving objects relative to the vehicle.

# Vehicle Peripheral Moving Object Detection Device

## Background and Technical Challenge

Detecting moving objects—particularly pedestrians and cyclists—in the area surrounding a vehicle presents significant technical challenges, especially in real-world driving conditions where visibility of these objects is frequently incomplete or obstructed. Traditional detection systems that rely on recognizing an object's full silhouette or complete body profile often fail when only a portion of a person or object is visible within the camera's field of view. This limitation becomes particularly problematic in cluttered urban environments, parking structures, intersections, or situations where pedestrians are partially occluded by other vehicles, structures, or objects at the periphery of the vehicle's sensing range.

## Device Configuration and Operation

To address these challenges, the disclosed device incorporates two primary functional units working in coordination.

**Image Acquisition Unit**: This component is responsible for capturing image data representing the peripheral area surrounding the vehicle. It may utilize one or more cameras positioned at strategic locations on the vehicle body to provide comprehensive coverage of blind spots, side zones, front, and rear areas. The acquired images serve as the raw visual input for subsequent processing stages.

**Image Extraction Unit**: Building upon the captured peripheral images, this unit performs a critical segmentation function by isolating specific portions of any detected moving objects within the image data. Rather than requiring a complete, unobstructed view of an entire moving object, the extraction unit is specifically configured to identify and extract:

- The upper-body portion of a moving object (such as the head, shoulders, and torso region)
- The lower-body portion of a moving object (such as the legs and lower torso region)
- Combinations thereof, depending on what portions are actually visible

Critically, this extraction capability accounts for both **complete views** and **partial views** of each body region. For example, if only a fraction of a pedestrian's upper body is visible due to partial occlusion by a parked vehicle, the image extraction unit can still identify and extract this partial upper-body segment as valid data for further analysis, rather than discarding it due to incompleteness.

## Enhanced Detection Through Granular Analysis

This body-region-based extraction methodology directly supports the **moving object information determination unit**, which utilizes the extracted upper-body and/or lower-body image segments to assess:

1. **Presence determination** – whether a moving object actually exists within the captured peripheral scene
2. **Position determination** – the spatial location and orientation of any detected moving object relative to the vehicle

Because the determination unit can operate on partial body-region data rather than requiring full-body visibility, the overall system achieves substantially improved robustness in scenarios where complete object visibility is not achievable. This is especially valuable in the following situations:

- Pedestrians emerging from behind parked cars, where initially only the upper body or head becomes visible
- Cyclists or pedestrians partially obscured by roadside infrastructure, signage, or other vehicles
- Objects at the edge of the camera's field of view, where only a portion of the body enters the frame
- Low-light or complex background conditions where partial-body features are more reliably detected than whole-body silhouettes

## Advantages

By decomposing the moving object detection problem into upper-body and lower-body components—and explicitly accommodating both complete and partial instances of each—the device achieves several key advantages over conventional whole-object detection approaches:

- **Increased detection reliability**: The system does not fail simply because a full-body view is unavailable, significantly reducing missed detections in obstructed scenarios.
- **Earlier hazard identification**: Partial visibility (e.g., a person's upper body appearing before their full form emerges from behind an obstruction) allows the system to flag potential hazards sooner rather than waiting for complete visual confirmation.
- **Improved accuracy in cluttered environments**: Segment-based analysis allows the determination unit to cross-reference upper and lower body cues even when neither is fully visible, improving confidence in genuinely ambiguous cases.
- **Real-world adaptability**: The approach is specifically designed to function under realistic driving conditions rather than idealized scenarios with unobstructed views.

## Conclusion

Overall, this device provides a technically robust solution to the persistent problem of moving object detection in vehicle peripheral zones. By enabling recognition based on partial as well as complete upper- and lower-body image data, the system meaningfully enhances the reliability, responsiveness, and safety benefits of vehicle-based moving object detection technology in complex, real-world driving environments.

# A Device For

The phrase "a device for" is one of the most quietly powerful constructions in the human vocabulary. It signals intention, problem-solving, and the fundamental human impulse to create tools that extend our capabilities beyond what nature gave us.

Every device begins with a gap—a need unmet, a task too difficult, a limitation waiting to be overcome. A device for measuring time freed civilizations from guessing at the sun's position. A device for communication collapsed distances that once took months to cross. A device for calculation turned complex mathematics into a matter of seconds.

What makes this phrase so compelling is its open-endedness. It invites completion: a device for *what*? The blank space after "for" is where imagination lives. It could be filled with the mundane (a device for opening jars) or the profound (a device for detecting gravitational waves). Both matter, because both represent the same underlying principle: identifying a problem and engineering a solution.

Throughout history, the greatest devices haven't just solved problems—they've revealed new ones. The telescope, a device for seeing distant objects, ended up showing us how much we didn't know about the universe. The printing press, a device for reproducing text, sparked social and political upheavals its inventor never anticipated. Devices don't just serve their stated purpose; they ripple outward, changing the world in ways their creators could scarcely predict.

Today, we live surrounded by devices for nearly everything: monitoring our health, translating languages in real time, automating decisions, connecting us to people and information instantaneously. The sheer proliferation raises important questions. Not every problem needs a device to solve it. Not every convenience is worth its hidden costs—environmental, social, or psychological.

Perhaps the most important skill for the future isn't inventing more devices, but discerning *which* problems truly deserve mechanical or digital solutions, and which are better addressed through human connection, patience, or acceptance. The best device, after all, might sometimes be no device at all—just a clearer understanding of what we actually need.

In the end, "a device for" is a phrase that captures both our ingenuity and our restlessness—a reminder that humans are, at our core, a species defined by the tools we build to reshape our world.

# Patent Claim Draft

## Claim 1

A vehicle-mounted pedestrian detection device comprising:

an image acquisition unit configured to acquire a peripheral image captured by a camera mounted on a vehicle;

a segmentation unit configured to define, within the peripheral image, a detection region including a candidate object, and to divide the detection region into at least an upper-body image segment corresponding to an upper-body portion of a pedestrian and a lower-body image segment corresponding to a lower-body portion of the pedestrian;

an upper-body determination unit configured to extract a first feature quantity from the upper-body image segment and to calculate a first likelihood value indicating a probability that the upper-body image segment represents an upper body of a pedestrian, based on the first feature quantity;

a lower-body determination unit configured to extract a second feature quantity from the lower-body image segment and to calculate a second likelihood value indicating a probability that the lower-body image segment represents a lower body of a pedestrian, based on the second feature quantity, the lower-body determination unit calculating the second likelihood value using a determination criterion different from that used by the upper-body determination unit; and

a pedestrian recognition unit configured to determine whether the candidate object is a pedestrian based on a combination of the first likelihood value and the second likelihood value,

wherein the pedestrian recognition unit determines that the candidate object is a pedestrian when the combination of the first likelihood value and the second likelihood value satisfies a predetermined condition, even when one of the first likelihood value and the second likelihood value alone does not satisfy a threshold for identifying a pedestrian.

## Claim 2 (Dependent)

The vehicle-mounted pedestrian detection device according to claim 1, wherein the pedestrian recognition unit is configured to determine that the candidate object is a pedestrian when the first likelihood value is equal to or greater than a first threshold and the second likelihood value is equal to or greater than a second threshold lower than a threshold normally required when the second likelihood value is evaluated independently.

## Claim 3 (Dependent)

The vehicle-mounted pedestrian detection device according to claim 1, wherein the segmentation unit is configured to set a boundary between the upper-body image segment and the lower-body image segment based on an estimated position of a waist of the pedestrian, the estimated position being determined according to a size of the detection region.

## Claim 4 (Dependent)

The vehicle-mounted pedestrian detection device according to claim 1, wherein the first feature quantity includes at least one of a head shape feature, a shoulder line feature, and an arm swing feature extracted from the upper-body image segment, and the second feature quantity includes at least one of a leg shape feature and a stride pattern feature extracted from the lower-body image segment.

## Claim 5 (Dependent)

The vehicle-mounted pedestrian detection device according to claim 1, wherein the upper-body determination unit and the lower-body determination unit each comprise a discriminator trained using machine learning on a plurality of sample images corresponding respectively to upper-body portions and lower-body portions of pedestrians.

## Claim 6 (Dependent)

The vehicle-mounted pedestrian detection device according to claim 1, further comprising a vehicle control unit configured to execute at least one of a warning output and a vehicle braking operation when the pedestrian recognition unit determines that the candidate object is a pedestrian.

## Claim 7 (Dependent)

The vehicle-mounted pedestrian detection device according to claim 1, wherein the lower-body determination unit is configured to calculate the second likelihood value further based on a motion feature obtained from a plurality of the peripheral images captured at different time points, the motion feature representing a walking motion of the lower-body portion.

---

*Note: This is a draft template. Actual filing would require careful review by a licensed patent attorney/agent to ensure proper claim scope, support in the specification, compliance with jurisdiction-specific patent office requirements (e.g., USPTO, JPO, EPO formatting), and freedom-to-operate analysis relative to prior art such as existing pedestrian detection patent families (e.g., those from automotive OEMs and Tier 1 suppliers).*

A system for detecting the presence and position of a moving object near a vehicle, the system comprising:

The system of claim 1, wherein the one or more image sensors comprise at least one of a camera, an infrared sensor, or a time-of-flight sensor mounted on an exterior portion of the vehicle.

A method for detecting the presence and position of a moving object near a vehicle, the method comprising:
